Top of the Morning
 

Photo illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Photo: Daniel Maletzki/EUS-Nachrichten/Getty Images
 

Nvidia this morning reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO, effective immediately.

The big picture: This is what many in Silicon Valley had wanted, and what many on Wall Street thought was nearly impossible.

Investor reax: Nvidia shares are up around 30% on the news, representing around $900 billion in added value.

What they're saying: "I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," said Huang in the press release. "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."

  • Board chair Harvey Jones adds: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."
  • Also: "The Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

The intrigue: The company's independent investigation into Huang remains ongoing, which could put Nvidia in a box if its ultimate findings are in any way disqualifying for Huang.

  • Don't be surprised if Congress wants a peek at what Nvidia finds (and maybe at how hard it looked).
  • In terms of WH palace intrigue, it seems that Howard Lutnick bested Scott Bessent, which perhaps we should have seen coming yesterday when Bessent softened his earlier statements.

Zoom out: This is obviously huge news for AI trade momentum, but may just be a short-term sugar high.

  • Hyperscaler capex is flattening out, as AI profits remain elusive for almost all but those selling equipment to build and fill data centers (e.g., Nvidia).
  • Huang also is said to have become more conservative on investments in the weeks before his ouster, so his return doesn't necessarily mean a return to the Wild West of circular financing. Particularly as costs of capital increase.

Look ahead: Huang is expected to appear before House committees next week for a closed-door transcribed interview, and then at a future date for a public Senate Banking Committee hearing. All of that just got even more interesting.
 
 
The BFD
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

CrowdStrike (Nasdaq: CRWD) agreed to acquire cybersecurity firm Zscaler (Nasdaq: ZS) for around $43.9 billion in stock.

Why it's the BFD: Cyber consolidation is accelerating as companies seek to defend against both AI-enabled threats and AI-discovered security holes.

By the numbers: Zscaler shareholders will receive an implied value of $260.41 per share, which represents a 34% premium to Friday's closing price.

The bottom line: "The deal will pitch CrowdStrike into greater competition with Palo Alto Networks and Microsoft and underscores the shift toward a smaller number of companies protecting more of the world's computers and networks." — Ryan Gould and David Carnevali, Bloomberg

Final Numbers
 
Data: Financial Modeling Prep; Chart: Dan Primack/Axios

Global Payments shares spiked nearly 10% on Friday, after private equity firm GTCR confirmed in a regulatory filing that it's working on a take-private bid.

  • GTCR holds a 16.35% stake in Global Payments. It received the shares earlier this year via the $24.25 billion sale of Worldpay to Global Payments.
  • The deal reportedly could be valued at around $50 billion, although GTCR would need partners. There had been reports that CD&R was a possibility, but it seems to have since backed away.

Axios Pro's Ryan Lawler: "Global Payments shares had fallen since the Worldpay deal, and perhaps GTCR believes the market is underestimating what the combined business will do once fully integrated. Or that it could do a better job on the integration."
